Case report
A 41-year-old man presented to the accident and emergency
department following a fall and a 4-week history of progressive
lower back stiffness and bilateral leg weakness. He also reported a
3-month history of polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and fatigue.
Past medical history consisted of biopsy proven CD and dermati-
tis herpetiformis, both well controlled with a gluten-free diet and
dapsone. On examination, vitals were stable, and a rash consistent

with dermatitis herpetiformis was present on the trunk and exten-
sor surfaces of arms and legs. Neurological examination was limited
by the painful muscular spasms leading to generalised muscle stiff-
ness that was exacerbated by movement. When the spasms were

most intense, the posture was hyperlordotic and there was proxi-
mal muscle stiffness in the upper and lower limbs, manifested by
hyperextension. Reﬂexes, including plantar responses, and sensa-
tion were normal. There was no alteration in mental status and
breathing was not reported by the patient to be affected.
Plasma glucose was 36.4 mmol/l, pH 7.44, bicarbonate
24.4 mmol/l (normal range 18–24), serum ketonaemia with
/H9252-hydroxybutyrate of 3.4 mmol/l and HbA1c (DCCT aligned) was
8.0% at presentation. Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase
(anti-GAD) antibodies were sent for analysis in the immunology
laboratory in the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, United King-
dom (performed on July 2005) and returned positive, at a titre of
105 U/ml. The cut-off for this assay is <1 U/ml, with positive results
being from 1 to 300 U/ml.
The patient was commenced on a basal bolus insulin replace-
ment regime of novorapid and levemir to treat his hyperglycaemia.
Thyroid function tests revealed a pattern consistent with subclinical
hypothyroidism with a free thyroxine of 9.6 pmol/l (normal range
8–21) and a thyroid stimulating hormone of 5.46 mIU/l (normal
range 0.5–4.2). Anti thyroid peroxidase antibodies were positive at
105 U/ml (normal range 0–50).
Neurological investigations including serum B
12, MRI scans of
the brain and spinal cord were normal, with no evidence of a
demyelinating disorder or a space occupying lesion. CSF analy-

sis was acellular with a normal protein concentration (46 mg/dl;
normal range 15–45 mg/dl) but anti-GAD antibodies were strongly
positive at 61 U/ml.
A clinical diagnosis of SPS was made and the patient was com-
menced on a diazepam infusion, followed by plasmapheresis, and
later intravenous immunoglobulin (IV Ig) to good clinical effect.
Tumour markers including synaptophysin, a CT scan of the
thorax, abdomen and pelvis were performed to exclude a parane-
oplastic phenomenon and all were normal. Following 48 h of IV Ig,
serum anti-GAD antibodies fell to 4 U/ml.
HLA typing revealed our patient to be HLA-DR/H92521 0301/0305 and
HLA-DQ/H92521 02 positive.
The patient is currently treated with diazepam and baclofen for
his painful muscular spasms, and mycophenylate as an immuno-
modulatory agent. His symptoms have improved greatly and he has
been able to return to work.
